Transducers
Transducers in JavaScript: map and filter without intermediate arrays, reducers and reducer transformers, step order in R.compose, R.transduce and R.into.

Understand why a map and filter chain creates intermediate arrays, learn to write transducers as reducer transformers, compose them with compose, use R.transduce and R.into, and judge when it pays off.
text

A map and filter chain reads well, but it has a cost. Each step walks the whole array and creates a new one. filter(isEven), map(square), filter(isBig) means three passes and three new arrays, two of them intermediate: they are needed only as input for the next step. In the "Performance" lesson we already counted this overhead in callback calls; now let's count the arrays too.
code

You could merge all the steps into a single reduce, as in the exercise of the "Performance" lesson, but then they would fuse into one callback and stop being separate functions. Transducers give you both: the steps stay separate and composable, and the data goes through them in a single pass, with no intermediate arrays. The idea comes from Clojure, where Rich Hickey proposed transducers in 2014.
heading
A reducer and a reducer transformer

A reducer is the function that reduce takes: (acc, x) => newAcc. It receives the accumulated value and the next element and returns the new accumulated value. Summing is a reducer, and so is appending an element to an array.

A transducer is a reducer transformer: a function that takes a reducer and returns a new reducer. mapping(f) turns a reducer into one that applies f to the element first, and filtering(pred) turns it into one that lets only matching elements through to the original reducer. Neither of them knows what the reducer does: collects an array, computes a sum or builds a string.
Composing transducers

A transducer is a function of one argument, so transducers compose with compose. The order of writing is unusual here: in compose(filtering(isEven), mapping(square)) the elements are filtered first and only then squared. The steps run left to right, as in pipe.

Here is why. compose does apply functions right to left, but it applies them to the reducer, not to the data. First mapping(square) wraps the final reducer, then filtering(isEven) wraps the result. The leftmost wrapper ends up outermost, and every element reaches it first. The wrappers are built right to left, and the data goes through them left to right.
Transducers in Ramda

In Ramda, map, filter, take and a number of other list functions work as transducers if you call them without data and pass the result to R.transduce or R.into. R.transduce(xform, reducer, init, list) is a fold like our transduce: you supply the reducer and the initial value. R.into(acc, xform, list) picks the reducer from its first argument: elements are appended to an array, concatenated to a string, or have their properties or [key, value] pairs copied into an object. Note that in Ramda 0.32 only the type of the first argument is used, and its contents do not make it into the result: R.into([1, 2], R.map(R.inc), [3]) returns [4], not [1, 2, 4]. So pass an empty value: [], '' or {}. The Ramda docs call an object with the @@transducer/init, @@transducer/step and @@transducer/result methods a transformer, and a function that takes such a transformer and returns a new one a transducer. The idea is the same, just with an object instead of a reducer function.
When it pays off

On a full pass transducers don't reduce the number of step calls: every element goes through every step it reaches, just as in the chain. The gain is elsewhere. There are no intermediate arrays and no extra passes. The fold can stop early, as with R.take. The same transformation works with any reducer and any source Ramda's fold understands: an array, an iterable such as a Set or a generator, or an object with a reduce method.

This shows on large collections, long chains and early stopping. For an array of a hundred elements and two steps, a map and filter chain is easier to read and fast enough. ES2025 gave iterators their own lazy map, filter and take methods: they also handle elements one by one, with no intermediate arrays. Transducers differ in that they separate the transformation both from the data source and from the way the result is collected. As in the "Performance" lesson, check the gain by measuring: count arrays and calls, or repeat time measurements, rather than relying on a single run.
